title: The Language of Birds (简体中文)
summary: Akbar asks Birbal to interpret the screeching of two owls on a ruined wall. Birbal delivers a powerful political parable on governance and taxation. [ZH]
full_text:
While riding through the countryside outside Agra on an evening hunt, Emperor Akbar and Birbal passed an abandoned village. The houses were ruined shells, the fields overgrown with weeds, and the irrigation canals choked with mud. Perched upon the crumbling mud wall of an old house, two large horned owls were screeching loudly at each other: *Hoo-hoo! Hoot-hoot!*

Akbar reined in his stallion. In a whimsical mood, he turned to Birbal and said: 'Birbal, ancients claimed that King Solomon understood the language of birds. You are known as the wisest man in Hindustan. Tell me—what are those two owls arguing about so fiercely?'

Birbal listened intently to the owls' cries, nodding his head with a grave expression.

'Well, Birbal?' Akbar pressed. 'Do you understand their speech?'

Birbal sighed with heavy sorrow: 'Sire, it is a delicate domestic dispute regarding a wedding.'

'A wedding between owls?' Akbar asked, amused. 'Explain it to me!'

Birbal replied: 'Your Majesty, the owl on the left is the father of a young male owl. The owl on the right is the father of a young female owl. They are arranging a marriage between their children.

'The father of the bride owl is saying: "I will gladly give my daughter to your son in marriage, on one strict condition: as a bridal dowry, you must give me fifty ruined, abandoned villages where my daughter can hunt mice in peace!"

'And what does the groom's father reply?' Akbar asked.

Birbal looked into Akbar's eyes with deep solemnity:

'Sire, the father of the groom owl laughs with joy and replies: "Fifty ruined villages? My dear friend, as long as our Emperor Akbar allows his corrupt tax collectors to oppress the peasants and rob the farmers, I can easily promise you five hundred ruined villages before next winter!"'

The words struck Emperor Akbar like a slap across the face. He looked at the desolate houses, the cracked earth, and the empty granaries of the ruined village. The romantic veil of imperial glory fell away, revealing the suffering of his subjects under greedy regional governors.

Tears sprang to the Emperor's eyes. He turned his horse back toward Agra that very hour, dismissed the oppressive tax collectors, lowered agricultural taxes, and funded the restoration of ruined villages, thanking Birbal for using the voice of owls to speak the truth to power.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
